items.question: A marketplace classifies seller reviews for policy violations at roughly 4 million reviews a month, all processed on a nightly schedule with no user waiting. Each request is a 2,400-token instruction block of policy definitions, worked examples and output schema, followed by the review bundle — the review text plus the order record and the buyer-seller message thread — which averages 9,600 tokens and is unique to each request. Outputs are a short structured verdict. An engineer proposes enabling prompt caching on the instruction block as the main cost initiative for the quarter.

options.A: Enable it and add a second breakpoint after the review bundle so the whole request is covered by the cache.
options.B: Reverse the order so the review bundle leads and the instruction block follows, improving locality for the cache.
options.C: Skip caching and raise the output allowance instead so each of the 4 million classifications completes in one call.
options.D: Enable caching, but note that only a fifth of each request is reusable; the bigger levers are tier and batch.

items.question: A retail analytics team submits a 90,000-request batch each night. Last night the submission call failed with a network error after the request body had been sent, so the client has no confirmation of whether the batch was registered. The on-call operator must act before the morning deadline. A duplicate batch would double the night's spend and produce two result sets the loader cannot tell apart. What should the operator do next?

options.A: Resubmit immediately, since a duplicate batch is cheaper than missing the deadline; delete the surplus afterwards.
options.B: List the jobs the batch service registered around the failed submission and match one by creation time and request count; submit only if none is found.
options.C: Wait for the usual turnaround window to elapse and resubmit only if no results have appeared by then.
options.D: Resubmit under a new identifier and reconcile the two result sets against the source records in the morning.

items.question: A publishing house's manuscript-assessment service works on books of 40 to 80 MB. It splits each book into 200 KB slices and pushes every slice through the company's central model gateway, so a single assessment carries an entire manuscript across the gateway in several hundred calls. The gateway now dominates memory usage in its cluster, its audit store is growing far faster than forecast, and p99 gateway latency has degraded for the six other teams that share it. What should the architect change?

options.A: Grant the manuscript service a direct path to the provider that bypasses the gateway, since its payload profile is unlike everyone else's.
options.B: Increase the gateway's memory limits and expand the audit store's capacity so the manuscript workload fits comfortably alongside the other six teams.
options.C: Have the application extract the relevant sections before the call, and have the gateway audit a digest and a reference, not the body.
options.D: Compress request bodies in transit so that both the gateway's memory footprint and the audit store's growth rate are meaningfully reduced.

items.question: A telco processes roughly 3 million customer chat events a day through a Claude-based intent classifier. Ordering matters strictly within a single customer's conversation, because a later message can supersede an earlier one, but ordering between different customers is irrelevant. A single strictly ordered queue cannot sustain the volume. What design satisfies both requirements?

options.A: Use a single strictly ordered queue with many more consumers, since ordering is a property of the queue itself rather than of how it is consumed.
options.B: Use an unordered queue and have each consumer buffer briefly and sort the events it receives by producer timestamp before calling the classifier.
options.C: Partition the stream by customer identifier so ordering holds within each partition while partitions are consumed in parallel, provisioning enough partitions up front to carry the volume.
options.D: Use an unordered queue with a global sequence number, and have consumers buffer any event that arrives ahead of the next expected number until the missing one lands.

items.question: An agent harness executes the `tool_use` blocks in an assistant turn concurrently by default. Which TWO conditions in a given batch require the harness to serialise it instead? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Two calls mutate the same record and neither carries a version the handler can check.
options.B: Two calls are routed to the same downstream inventory service over one connection pool.
options.C: Two calls read the same record and no call in the batch modifies it.
options.D: The downstream system requires the operations to be applied in a defined order.
options.E: The batch contains more than three tool calls in the one assistant turn.

items.question: A boutique wealth manager's client-briefing assistant handles about 300 requests a month — roughly ten a day. Its quality alert compares each day's adviser edit rate against a fixed baseline of 0.18 and fires when the day's figure exceeds 0.25. It fires roughly twice a week, and every investigation so far has found nothing — the following day returns to normal. The team is losing confidence in the metric. What should change?

options.A: Raise the alert boundary from 0.25 to 0.35 so that ordinary day-to-day variation at this volume no longer crosses it.
options.B: Alert on the absolute count of edited briefings per day rather than the rate, which removes the instability introduced by a small and variable daily denominator.
options.C: Evaluate the proxy over a window long enough to accumulate a stable sample and use bounds that widen as the sample shrinks, rather than a fixed daily boundary.
options.D: Stop alerting on the proxy and move it to the monthly operational review, where a whole month of traffic gives a reading reliable enough to act on with confidence.

items.question: A gaming platform maintains an adversarial suite of 900 prompts across nine harm categories for the assistant that helps moderators draft enforcement notices. Results are reported to leadership as a single number — 97% blocked — and the release gate requires at least 95%. The trust and safety director asks whether this gate is fit for purpose. What is the main weakness?

options.A: A single category can be failing a quarter of its prompts while the aggregate still reads 97% and clears the gate; the gate needs per-category rates with severity-weighted floors instead.
options.B: Nine hundred prompts is too small a sample for a safety claim, and the suite should be expanded by an order of magnitude before it gates anything.
options.C: The suite is static across releases, so the gate should be regenerated from scratch each time to stop prompts being tuned against known attack strings.
options.D: The threshold is too low for a safety control, and raising the aggregate floor from 95% to 99% blocked would give the gate real teeth.

items.question: An industrial equipment manufacturer generates field-service reports from technician notes plus retrieved excerpts of service manuals. A cost programme removed the few-shot examples and compressed the retrieved excerpts; token spend per report fell by 40% and the aggregate eval score was unchanged. Two months later the warranty team finds that reports increasingly cite superseded part numbers, which invalidates the warranty claims built from them. (Choose TWO.) Which two measurements, in place at the time of the change, would have exposed the regression before the warranty team found it?

options.A: A per-report token count and cost dashboard with an alert when either moves outside its expected band, giving early visibility of the change's effect.
options.B: A field-level check of every cited part number against the current-versus-superseded status the parts master holds for it, scored as a pass rate on the same report set before and after the change.
options.C: A grounding check confirming that each part number cited in the report appears in the excerpt the report was generated from, run on the compressed and uncompressed pipelines over identical inputs.
options.D: A latency breakdown by pipeline stage, to confirm that compression moved time out of generation without pushing it into the retrieval and ranking stages, and that the p95 for report production stayed inside the field team's budget.
options.E: An increase in the judge model's sampling temperature, so that near-identical reports receive a wider spread of scores and small differences become visible.

items.question: A game publisher's player-support agent holds sessions that often run for hours. To control cost the team added context compaction: once a session passes a token threshold, earlier turns are replaced by a running summary. Spend per session fell 30%. The single-turn eval suite is unchanged, and the production audit — which samples individual responses uniformly across all traffic and scores them — is also unchanged. Player complaints that the agent 'forgets what I told it' have tripled. Which diagnostic localises the effect using data the team already holds?

options.A: Re-slice the existing audit scores by player tier, since complaint volume is concentrated among the most engaged players and the effect should be visible there.
options.B: Grade each running summary against the turns it replaced, using a fixed checklist of facts a player has stated, to establish how much information the summariser drops at each compaction step and whether the loss grows with session length.
options.C: Re-slice the existing audit scores by each response's position relative to the first compaction event in its session, since a uniform sample over responses mixes turns that sit behind a summary with the many that never do, averaging any post-compaction effect away.
options.D: Re-run the single-turn eval suite against the compacted and uncompacted pipelines with a larger sample, to detect a smaller effect than the current suite can resolve.

items.question: An HR-tech company tracks a quarterly pass-rate trend for its interview-summary feature, sourced from an eval set that engineers edit in place as they add cases. Last month someone removed 30 items they judged unrealistic. The trend chart shows a four-point jump in the same period, and nobody can now say whether the jump came from a prompt change or from the removal. Which practices would have prevented the ambiguity? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Keep the eval set in the same repository as the prompt so the two always change together in a single reviewed commit.
options.B: Publish each state of the eval set as an immutable artefact with its own identifier and record that identifier alongside every score, so the chart refuses to plot two different sets as one continuous line.
options.C: Rescale historical scores to the new item count whenever items are removed, so the quarterly trend line stays continuous.
options.D: Freeze the eval set permanently at its first version, since any subsequent addition or removal makes the trend uninterpretable.
options.E: Whenever the set changes, re-score the unchanged prompt against both the old and the new set and publish the difference, so the step the edit contributes is measured separately from the prompt's.

items.question: A tax agency is migrating its 1,100 contact-centre agents from a keyword search tool to a Claude-based knowledge assistant. Training takes two hours per agent, and the agency cannot release more than 60 agents a week from the floor without breaching its published service level. The filing deadline is eighteen weeks away and the six weeks before it are peak, when call volume triples. The legacy search tool's support contract ends seven weeks after the filing deadline and cannot be renewed. Which migration plan fits the constraints?

options.A: Raise the weekly release to 100 agents so all 1,100 are trained before peak begins, accepting a temporary service-level dip during the run-up.
options.B: Cut every agent over at week ten using a condensed one-hour session, so the whole floor is on a single tool throughout the peak period.
options.C: Train and migrate as many agents as the 60-a-week limit allows before peak, keep the legacy tool live for the remainder through the deadline, and finish the migration in the quiet weeks that follow.
options.D: Hold the entire migration until after the filing deadline so that no change of any kind lands near the busiest period of the year.

items.question: A waste management company's business case for a Claude-based route-exception triage system shows a three-year net benefit of £1.0m across fourteen assumptions. Sensitivity analysis shows that varying one of them — the automation rate, the share of exceptions closed without a dispatcher — between 45% and 75% swings the three-year net roughly linearly from −£0.2m to £2.6m. Every other assumption moves the result by less than £0.15m. The three-week pilot measured 58%, which is the rate the case assumes. How should the case go to the investment committee?

options.A: As the £1.0m three-year point estimate, with all fourteen assumptions documented in an appendix for any member who wishes to interrogate them.
options.B: Led by the automation rate: the pilot's 58% on a three-week basis, the break-even rate of roughly 47%, and a stage gate releasing the next tranche once confirmed.
options.C: As a Monte Carlo distribution over all fourteen assumptions, giving the committee a probability distribution over the three-year net rather than a single point figure.
options.D: Withheld until the pilot has run long enough for the automation rate to stabilise, since presenting a case that turns on an unstable input is premature.

items.question: A digital bank's platform team plans to tell the CFO that 'unit cost per thousand tokens fell 31% after the optimisation programme'. Over the same six months, monthly inference spend rose from £84,000 to £119,000, and monthly requests rose from 6.1 million to 12.6 million; average tokens per request were unchanged, so the same 31% improvement holds per request. What should the report say?

options.A: Cost per request fell from £0.0138 to £0.0094 while volume more than doubled, so total monthly spend rose 42% to £119,000.
options.B: The 31% unit improvement alone, since total spend is a function of demand and demand is set by product, not by the platform team.
options.C: The increase in total spend alone, since that is the figure the CFO's budget carries and unit improvements are an internal engineering matter.
options.D: The 31% unit improvement together with the spend the bank would have incurred at the old unit cost, presenting the difference as a saving delivered.

items.question: Why is cost per resolved case a better executive metric for a Claude-based support deflection system than cost per API call?

options.A: Because escalated conversations stay in its numerator, so abandoning a hard case mid-way worsens the number.
options.B: Because it produces a smaller headline number and is therefore easier to get through budget approval.
options.C: Because per-call costs move with the provider's published pricing, which is outside the team's control.
options.D: Because executives are unfamiliar with token-based units and prefer metrics denominated in cases.

items.question: A pet insurer's marketing team wants the launch page for its Claude-based claims assistant to read 'instant decisions on every claim'. In production, 22% of claims are deferred to a human assessor with a stated two-working-day turnaround, and a further 4% are stopped by a guardrail and re-routed. Launch is in six days. What is the best next step?

options.A: Approve the copy: 74% of claims do receive an instant decision, and launch copy is understood to describe the intended experience rather than a guarantee.
options.B: Ask marketing to drop every reference to decision speed and describe the assistant's capabilities in general terms instead of numbers.
options.C: Escalate the wording to the legal team for a view on whether it is misleading, and let them determine the final launch copy.
options.D: Give marketing accurate wording backed by the figures: instant decisions on around three quarters of claims, most of the rest within two working days.

items.question: A telecommunications provider proposes a single acceptance criterion for its chat assistant pilot: containment rate of at least 60%, where containment means the chat ended without transfer to a human agent. Discovery finds that in 200 transcripts from a vendor demo deployment, 31% of contained chats were followed by the same customer contacting again within 48 hours. What is the most serious defect in this as the sole acceptance criterion?

options.A: Sixty percent is unrealistic for a first pilot and should be reset to the level comparable operator deployments achieve in their first year.
options.B: Containment cannot be computed automatically from the chat platform and would need manual review of every transcript, making the criterion impractical.
options.C: Containment should be reported per intent, so that chats about intents the assistant was never designed to resolve are removed from the denominator before the 60% target is applied.
options.D: Containment counts the absence of a transfer, not whether the problem was solved; it must be paired with a repeat-contact resolution measure.

items.question: A telecommunications group's AI council triages roughly forty candidate use cases each quarter. Which THREE findings should disqualify a candidate at the triage gate, rather than being admitted to design as a managed risk? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: There is no way, even in hindsight and with the full case file, to determine whether a given output was correct.
options.B: The source data sits in a mainframe with no API, so a nightly batch extract into the group data lake would have to be built.
options.C: No named business owner has been identified as accountable for the outcome metric the candidate claims to move.
options.D: The current process has never been formally measured, though two years of case-management timestamps exist from which a baseline can be built in discovery.
options.E: The output is an exact figure fixed by a regulator's published formula and must be reproducible on demand.

items.question: A freight brokerage exposes a shipment-exception triage endpoint to its carrier partners under a 2,000 ms p95 contractual budget. Measured end-to-end p95 today is 1,780 ms, leaving 220 ms of p95 headroom. The mean stage breakdown from tracing is: auth and routing 20 ms, retrieval from the exceptions index 120 ms, a single Sonnet-tier call 960 ms, response shaping 40 ms, egress 40 ms — a 1,180 ms end-to-end mean. Product now wants the exception classified into one of 40 categories *before* retrieval, so retrieval can be filtered by category. The prototype classifier is a second model call on the same tier that emits a short justification plus the label, and it measures 500 ms p95 and 320 ms mean. Means do compose additively, so inserting the stage serially moves the end-to-end mean from 1,180 ms to 1,500 ms, a 27% shift on a path whose p95 already sits within 220 ms of contract. Percentiles do not compose that way, so the team cannot subtract the stage's 500 ms p95 from the 220 ms of headroom and declare a breach — but it also has no measurement showing the contract still holds. What is the best design response?

options.A: Re-implement the classifier on the fastest tier, capped at a single label token and no justification, then re-measure end to end before committing.
options.B: Cache the classification in the existing Redis layer keyed on shipment id, so most exception events find a warm entry and skip the classifier call.
options.C: Issue the classifier call concurrently with retrieval so the two stages overlap, discarding the retrieval result whenever the returned category does not match.
options.D: Convert the endpoint to an accepted-then-callback contract with a webhook per carrier partner, so the p95 budget covers only the acknowledgement.

items.question: A pharmacy benefit manager is reviewing a prior-authorisation assistant against a 2,000 ms p95 budget. The team's design document adds the measured p95 of each non-overlapping trace span — request validation 90 ms, member and formulary retrieval 260 ms, the model call 1,820 ms, response assembly 140 ms — for a total of 2,310 ms, and concludes the design cannot meet the budget. A shadow deployment carrying mirrored production traffic reports a measured end-to-end p95 of 1,690 ms. The spans do not overlap and the clocks are synchronised. Which reading of this is correct?

options.A: The shadow figure is optimistic because mirrored traffic under-represents the real request mix; the additive 2,310 ms estimate should be treated as the planning number.
options.B: The discrepancy indicates instrumentation loss in the model-call span; the team should re-instrument and re-derive the budget from the corrected stage sum.
options.C: Both figures are valid for different purposes: the sum is the true p95 and the shadow figure is the p50, so the design meets the budget only half the time.
options.D: Percentiles are not additive: 2,310 ms is a request at the tail of every stage at once, which is rare. The measured end-to-end p95 is the real number.

items.question: A transit authority's service-disruption assistant fans out to five subagents and synthesises their returns into a passenger advisory. Identical inputs replayed an hour apart produce advisories that emphasise different causes and occasionally reverse the recommended alternative route. Investigation shows the branches are appended to the aggregator's prompt in completion order, which varies run to run. Throughput requirements rule out running the branches sequentially. What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Assemble the aggregator's input in canonical branch order rather than arrival order, so the same set of returns always produces the same prompt.
options.B: Set the aggregator's sampling temperature to zero, treating that as a determinism guarantee for the synthesis step.
options.C: Add a judge agent that generates two candidate advisories, compares them against the five branch returns, and selects the better one.
options.D: Have each subagent stamp its return with a completion timestamp so the aggregator can record the true ordering in the trace.

items.question: A medical device manufacturer screens 30,000 customer complaints a month for potentially reportable adverse events. A missed reportable event costs an estimated $2,400 in regulatory remediation; an unnecessary referral costs $18 of specialist review time, and the review team can absorb up to 4,000 referrals a month. Historical audit puts the true reportable rate at 1% of complaints, or about 300 a month. Two operating points have been measured on a held-out set. Threshold 1: 0.12% of items are false negatives, 3% are false positives. Threshold 2: 0.04% false negatives, 11% false positives. Which should be chosen?

options.A: Threshold 1, because its total error rate of 3.12% is far below threshold 2's 11.04%, and overall accuracy is the metric the regulator's inspectors will ask about.
options.B: Neither as measured: a third operating point between the two should be found and measured before committing, since both look extreme.
options.C: Threshold 2, because expected monthly cost is about $88,200 against $102,600 for threshold 1, and its 3,588 referrals fit inside the 4,000 review capacity.
options.D: Threshold 1, because threshold 2's 3,588 referrals a month consume most of the review team's monthly capacity and leave no room for volume growth.

items.question: A commercial insurer triages first-notice-of-loss submissions with a cascade: a Haiku-tier first pass at a measured $0.0008 per call handles the submission, and low-confidence cases escalate to an Opus-tier adjudication at a measured $0.019 per call. At launch, 25% escalated. Since a new marine cargo product went live, the escalation rate has settled at 58%. Finance has flagged the cost line and asked whether the cascade should be abandoned in favour of sending everything to the Opus tier. Which characterisation of the drift is accurate?

options.A: The cascade has crossed over: at 58% escalation the cheap first pass is pure overhead on top of an adjudication that happens anyway, so routing everything straight to the Opus tier costs less.
options.B: Blended cost per submission has more than doubled, but the cascade still runs about 38% below flat Opus-tier routing, with break-even near a 96% escalation rate; the real change is that 58% of submissions now make two serial calls.
options.C: Cost per submission is essentially unchanged, because the Haiku-tier first pass is negligible next to the adjudication call and only the escalated share ever moved the line.
options.D: The cascade saves the same proportion it always did, because both tiers price linearly per submission and the ratio between the first-pass and adjudication rates is fixed.

items.question: An online marketplace onboards about 5,000 new sellers a week. A Claude step assesses each application against listing policy, and the risk team then reviews every case before the seller may list; the median wait is 26 hours and is the largest single cause of onboarding drop-off. The risk team has depth capacity for 1,000 cases a week. Sellers can be suspended and their listings removed at any time, and the marketplace already does this routinely with same-day effect. How should the review be positioned?

options.A: Keep the synchronous gate and grow the risk team fivefold until it can review all 5,000 cases a week within a few hours.
options.B: Auto-approve the applications the model scores as confident and hold the remainder in the existing synchronous review queue.
options.C: Let sellers list immediately on the model's assessment, and run human review asynchronously against a risk-ranked queue.
options.D: Let all sellers list immediately and retire the human review step entirely, relying on post-listing monitoring and buyer reports.

items.question: An in-path output guardrail is adding materially to p95 latency on a customer-facing Claude feature, and the product owner wants the time back. Responses are generated per request against per-user context and are effectively unique — telemetry records an exact-text repeat in well under 1% of traffic. Which TWO changes reduce the guardrail's latency contribution while keeping it a preventive control? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Apply the guardrail to a randomly sampled 10% of responses and let the remaining 90% through to customers unchecked.
options.B: Evaluate the guardrail on the smallest unit it can validly assess, so checking overlaps generation rather than following it.
options.C: Move the guardrail to run after delivery and retract any response in the widget that subsequently fails the check.
options.D: Run the guardrail's independent sub-checks concurrently rather than chained, so the cost is the slowest check not their sum.
options.E: Cache guardrail verdicts keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the response text so that repeated responses skip the check entirely.

items.question: Which THREE statements are true of the isolation between an orchestrator and a subagent it invokes? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The subagent starts from a copy of the caller's context window, so anything the caller had already loaded is available to the branch without being restated.
options.B: Material the subagent read is unavailable to the caller unless it was deliberately returned or persisted somewhere the caller can reach.
options.C: Constraints the caller established earlier in its conversation are invisible to the subagent unless the handoff carries them.
options.D: Caller and subagent draw on a single shared context window, so a long branch reduces the caller's remaining headroom.
options.E: An instruction embedded in content the subagent read can influence the caller only if it reaches the caller through the returned result.

items.question: A benefits agency's assistant runs three safety layers: an input classifier, an output classifier, and an independent intent check on proposed actions. Together they now cost more per request than the generation itself, and the programme's annual budget is fixed and already committed. The safety lead is asked to reduce guardrail spend by roughly a third without an unmeasured loss of coverage. What should be done first?

options.A: Move all three layers to the cheapest model tier, keeping the architecture intact and accepting a uniform reduction in classifier quality across the whole stack.
options.B: Remove the output classifier, since the input classifier and the intent check both act earlier in the request path and prevention is preferable to detection.
options.C: Measure each layer's unique contribution on held-out traffic and remove or narrow the layer with the least unique coverage.
options.D: Run the full stack on a sampled 20% of traffic and the input classifier alone on the remainder, which cuts guardrail spend without removing any layer entirely.

items.question: A hospital group's referral intake handles about 2,000 external referral letters a day, arriving as emailed PDFs from practices outside its control. An agent reads each letter and books an appointment in the scheduling system, which it can write to directly. Clinical governance will not accept a design where letter content can steer a booking, and the volume rules out human confirmation of every extracted field, by a clinician or by anyone else. How should the components be arranged?

options.A: Give the planning agent the raw letter text but restrict its tool set to create and amend operations on the scheduling system only, so the worst case is a mis-booked appointment.
options.B: Send the letter to two different models in parallel and proceed only when their extractions agree, treating any disagreement as a signal that the document may have been tampered with.
options.C: Have the agent present every extracted field to the intake clerk for confirmation before the booking call is made, so a human always stands between the letter and the scheduling system whatever the letter contains.
options.D: Route the letter to a reader model that has no tools and returns only typed values, and have the privileged planner work from those values as opaque variables without ever receiving the letter text.

items.question: A property-listings portal's assistant can return an owner's contact details to verified estate agents. Every individual lookup is legitimate and authorised. A risk review is concerned about an agent account retrieving thousands of owner records one at a time to build a marketing list. Which two controls address this? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Apply per-principal volume and velocity limits to the lookup tool, with alerting when a session's count of distinct records retrieved departs from normal working patterns.
options.B: Require the model to include a justification string with each lookup call, stored alongside the result so that the stated purpose is available for later review.
options.C: Return owner contact details only after a deterministic check that the requesting agent holds an active mandate on that specific property.
options.D: Add a fixed delay between repeated lookups within a single conversation session, the counter resetting whenever a new session is opened, so that collecting many records in one sitting is slow.
options.E: Log every lookup with the calling agent, the record retrieved and a timestamp, and review those logs monthly for unusual patterns.

items.question: A Dutch contact-centre operator's product team proposes a feature that infers each caller's emotional state from the live transcript and displays a running frustration score to the agent handling the call. Those inferred scores are then aggregated per agent and presented to supervisors as a per-worker measure of the emotional tone each agent's calls produce, used in individual coaching and performance conversations. The team has drafted a design and asks the architect to review the guardrails, the bias evaluation plan and the human-review step. All employees and callers are in the EU. What should happen next?

options.A: Approve the design to proceed to build with the proposed guardrails and bias evaluation, and classify the feature formally once measured accuracy is available from the pilot.
options.B: Treat it as a high-risk employment system and begin the conformity workstream, since anything producing per-worker measures for supervisors sits in that tier.
options.C: Screen the proposal against the prohibited practices list before any further design work, because emotion inference used to characterise workers in the workplace is among the most restricted areas.
options.D: Consult the works council first and let their response determine the design, since employee representation is the binding constraint and the Act governs systems sold externally rather than used internally.

items.question: A Turkish conglomerate has acquired a 200-person insurtech. Due diligence covered financials, intellectual property and security, but not AI. On the first day of integration the acquirer finds four customer-facing AI features in production, none of them registered anywhere, one of which generates pricing recommendations that underwriters accept without change in most cases. The group standard requires all AI in the group to be registered and risk-tiered within ninety days of acquisition, and it reserves suspension of a live feature to the approval board on evidence of harm or of a breached obligation. No such evidence has emerged: the target reports no complaints, no loss events and no regulator contact on any of the four. Which TWO actions should be prioritised inside that window? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Register all four as use cases with a named accountable owner drawn from the group's structure, and tier them on consequence and autonomy.
options.B: Migrate all four features onto the acquirer's model gateway before the ninety days expire, so that they fall under central logging and credential control immediately.
options.C: Establish what the target's customer contracts and its own AI vendor contracts say about model data use, since those terms transferred with the business and now bind the group.
options.D: Suspend the pricing-recommendation feature until the acquirer's approval board has reviewed it, on the grounds that it affects customers and has never been assessed.
options.E: Require every engineer at the target to complete the group's AI policy training and sign the acceptable-use attestation within the first month of integration.

items.question: A Colombian retail group has an approved Claude-based complaint triage assistant running in its home market. It now wants to run the identical system — same code, same prompts, same model, same hosting — for a recently acquired Ecuadorian subsidiary. The group standard requires re-approval wherever the risk profile changes materially. Which TWO things must be assessed before the extension proceeds? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Whether the evaluation set represents the subsidiary's complaint mix, product range and language use, since the recorded performance was measured entirely on home-market cases.
options.B: Whether the underlying model performs equivalently at the higher request volume, since combined traffic across both markets will roughly double.
options.C: Who the accountable owner is in the subsidiary, and whether the escalation route to a human complaint handler exists and is staffed there.
options.D: Whether the subsidiary's staff have completed the group's AI policy training before the assistant is made available to them.
options.E: Whether the system should be rebuilt on the subsidiary's own infrastructure so that the two markets do not share a technical dependency.

items.question: A pharmacovigilance team codes adverse-event narratives to a controlled vocabulary. A newer, higher-capability tier scores clearly better on published reasoning benchmarks. The team ran its own blind eval on 600 labelled narratives: agreement is 91.4% on the current tier and 91.7% on the new one, with overlapping confidence intervals. Slice analysis shows the new tier fixes 6 of the current tier's 52 failures and introduces 5 new ones. Measured cost per case is 3.1x and p95 latency 2.4x. The programme director wants to upgrade 'to stay current'. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Discard the internal eval on the grounds that 600 narratives cannot resolve a gap that a benchmark of tens of thousands of items detected, and follow the benchmark.
options.B: Upgrade, because benchmark gains generally transfer to production tasks once the prompt has been retuned and the few-shot examples refreshed for the newer tier.
options.C: Stay on the current tier, log the eval as the decision record, and re-test when the failure profile, the vocabulary or the eval set changes.
options.D: Upgrade only the cases the current tier gets wrong, routed by a confidence signal, so the higher tier is paid for on 8.7% of volume.

items.question: A wealth manager's advice-drafting assistant produces suitability notes. The regulator requires the firm to show, for any note, exactly which client facts and which product documents informed it, for six years after issue. Today context is assembled dynamically from a CRM and a product library, and the team logs only the final note and the adviser's prompt. The regulator has announced a thematic audit for next year that will sample notes and require the firm to evidence what informed each one. What should the team do next?

options.A: Plan to re-run the assistant against the CRM and product library at audit time, reproducing any note the regulator samples to show how it was derived.
options.B: Log the model version and sampling parameters going forward, so that any note can be regenerated deterministically on demand.
options.C: Ask the CRM and product library owners to retain their full change histories, so that the inputs to any sampled note can be inferred retrospectively.
options.D: Persist, alongside each note, either the fully assembled prompt or a manifest naming every context block with its source identifier and version.

items.question: A rail operator is writing the compaction policy for a long-running incident-management agent before it goes to production. The policy is scoped to how a compaction is performed; when a run should be abandoned and escalated, and what the agent costs to operate, are settled in separate documents. Which THREE elements must this policy specify for an engineer to implement it without further decisions? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The trigger condition, expressed in measured context utilisation with reserved headroom rather than in turn or tool-call counts.
options.B: The required contents of the summary, naming the fields that must survive and which of them must survive verbatim.
options.C: The maximum number of compactions permitted per incident, after which the run is terminated and handed to a controller.
options.D: What is excluded from the compacted region — the system prompt, pinned reference material and the most recent turns.
options.E: The model tier permitted to serve the agent's own reasoning steps between compactions.

items.question: A manufacturing group runs Claude-based defect-report triage at roughly 900,000 requests a month. Capturing every trace with rendered prompts would cost more than the inference itself, so the platform team samples 1% of traces at the head. Quality engineers report the same frustration every time: whenever a customer-reported bad triage is investigated, that specific trace was not among the sampled ones. Which sampling change best fits this workload?

options.A: Raise head sampling from 1% to 10%: any given trace becomes ten times more likely to be captured, at one tenth of the cost of capturing every trace in full.
options.B: Keep head sampling at 1% but extend retention on the sampled traces from 90 days to seven years, so that any historical investigation always has some material to work from.
options.C: Adopt tail-based sampling: decide after the request completes, keeping traces that errored, ran long, or were flagged by a quality signal, plus a small random baseline.
options.D: Stop capturing traces and rely on the application's structured logs, which already record a line for the request and the response of every call.

items.question: A university admissions platform's Claude-based document-completeness checker scores 96% on a 500-case eval set assembled from historical applications. In the first week of the intake period, admissions staff report it misses genuinely missing documents in roughly one application in eight. The team re-runs the eval suite against the currently deployed prompt and still gets 96%. What is the most useful next step?

options.A: Move the checker to a higher model tier, since production inputs are evidently harder than the historical cases the eval set was built from.
options.B: Add the reported production failures to the eval set and re-run the suite, so that it reflects the reality admissions staff are experiencing during this intake week.
options.C: Lower the confidence threshold at which the checker flags an application as incomplete, trading a rise in false positives for fewer missed documents.
options.D: Sample the failing production applications and compare their composition against the eval set's, since a gap this wide points first at a difference between the two populations.

items.question: A bank's internal assistant for branch staff is exercised round the clock by a synthetic probe that submits reference questions every few minutes and checks the answers. At 23:50 the probe's answers begin arriving without the mandatory regulatory disclaimer that a post-processing step is supposed to append, and the quality monitor pages the on-call engineer automatically. Branches are closed and staff use the assistant only during branch hours, 08:00 to 18:00. The likely cause is a change that shipped at 18:00; the deploy pipeline requires two approvers and the second approver is unreachable overnight. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Disable the assistant with its feature flag now, record the flag state and the monitor's evidence, and hand a full brief to the morning team.
options.B: Escalate to wake a second approver and revert the 18:00 deploy tonight, since a missing regulatory disclaimer is a compliance breach and cannot wait.
options.C: Leave the assistant enabled, set an alarm for 07:00, and reassess before branches open so that no action is taken on incomplete information.
options.D: Downgrade the page to a ticket for the owning team's business hours, since no user is affected while every branch is closed.

items.question: A conglomerate's platform group publishes a shared Claude Code toolkit that twelve product teams have adopted. Publication is already gated on a test suite that exercises every hook, agent and command against a fresh checkout. On Tuesday they published an update that changed a hook's behaviour in a way the suite did not cover, and by mid-morning all twelve teams were blocked on the same failure. The immediate cause is understood, a corrected version is ready, and the affected teams have been unblocked. The head of platform engineering wants to know what changes so this cannot recur at this scale.

options.A: Extend the existing pre-publication suite until it covers the hook behaviour that slipped through, so a defect of this kind is caught upstream in future.
options.B: Have each adopting team disable the toolkit's hooks locally when a problem occurs, and publish a documented procedure so they can do it within minutes.
options.C: Withdraw the shared toolkit and let each product team own its own copy of the artefacts, so a single publication can never affect twelve teams simultaneously.
options.D: Change adoption so that each repository moves to a new version deliberately rather than automatically, with one team taking each release first.

items.question: A staffing platform's team merged a change adding a formatting hook to the repository's committed settings. Since the merge, every teammate's session reports a hook failure on each edit, because the hook invokes a binary at a path that exists only on the author's machine. The author is on leave. Work is continuing but the failures are noisy and two engineers have started ignoring all hook output. What should the team do next?

options.A: Change the hook to invoke the formatter through the repository's own tooling, and add a CI check that exercises the committed configuration in a fresh checkout.
options.B: Revert the merge to restore the previous configuration, and reopen the change when the author returns from leave and can test it on a colleague's machine.
options.C: Document the required binary in the repository's setup instructions and ask each engineer to install it, since the hook is correct and the environments are incomplete.
options.D: Move the hook from the committed settings into the author's personal configuration, so it stops affecting teammates while remaining available to whoever wants it.
